pass1.sentence: Whether a blood test needs preparation depends on the test, and the clinician who arranges it should say what applies.

pass1.sentence: For some tests the preparation is a period without food or drink other than water, and for others it can involve medicines such as anticoagulants.

pass1.sentence: Food and drink can change some results because nutrients from a meal may still be in the blood at the time of the test.

pass1.sentence: Some blood tests need preparation and many do not.

pass1.sentence: The NHS says your GP, nurse or specialist should tell you whether you need to prepare, so it is worth checking the appointment letter or asking when the test is booked.

pass1.sentence: For some tests, preparation means not eating or drinking anything other than water for a set time beforehand.

pass1.sentence: For others, it can mean pausing certain medicines, such as anticoagulants (medicines that thin the blood), but only when the clinician says so.

pass1.sentence: Fasting means going without food and drink, apart from water, for a period before the test.
pass1.note: Hospital leaflet and MedlinePlus: nutrients from food enter the bloodstream and may alter results; fasting length differs by test (leaflet lists different hours for glucose, lipids and glucose tolerance tests; no hours given here).

pass1.sentence: The reason is that nutrients from food enter the bloodstream and may still be there when the sample is taken, which can change the results of some blood tests.
pass1.note: Hospital leaflet and MedlinePlus: nutrients from food enter the bloodstream and may alter results; fasting length differs by test (leaflet lists different hours for glucose, lipids and glucose tolerance tests; no hours given here).

pass1.sentence: Practices that publish fasting advice usually mean plain water only on the morning of the test.
